audits.mathematicalReason: Classify the small cubes by position to avoid counting any cube twice. The pair of faces with shaded corner squares accounts for all 8 corner cubes. The pair with shaded edge-middle squares accounts for 2 × 4 = 8 edge-middle cubes. The checkerboard pair and the top/bottom pair each contribute two face-center cubes, giving 4 face-center cubes. Thus the total is 8 + 8 + 4 = 20. This classification-and-multiplication solution supports the proposed counting scope, with cube structure as supporting knowledge.

audits.mathematicalReason: Measure horizontal positions from the rectangle's left side AD. The upper chord endpoints have positions B = 4 and C = 9, so its midpoint has position 6.5. The perpendicular diameter theorem places the midpoints of the parallel chords BC and EF on the same perpendicular line. Since E has position 3, half of EF is 6.5 − 3 = 3.5. Therefore EF = 7. The rectangle properties and segment arithmetic support the assessed chord-midpoint theorem.

figureEvidence.fact: A, B, C lie on the rectangle's upper side, while D, E, F lie on its lower side; AD is perpendicular to these parallel sides.
B and C are the upper circle intersections, and E and F are the lower circle intersections, so BC and EF are parallel chords.

audits.mathematicalReason: Each diameter is 30, so AN = 45 and AP = 75. The tangent property gives PG perpendicular to AG, with PG = 15. Let H be the perpendicular projection of N onto AG. The right triangles ANH and APG are similar, hence NH = 15 × 45/75 = 9. Because the perpendicular from the center bisects chord EF, EF = 2 sqrt(15² − 9²) = 24. This directly supports the tangent and perpendicular-diameter scopes, with similarity and Pythagoras supporting the selected solution.

figureEvidence.fact: The three circles are consecutive along AD, with centers O, N, P on that line and shared diameter endpoints B and C.

audits.mathematicalReason: Drop perpendiculars from A and B to DC, meeting it at X and Y. The right triangle at C has hypotenuse 3 sqrt(2) and angle 45°, so BY = YC = 3. Thus AX = 3 as well. At D, DX = 3/tan(60°) = sqrt(3), while XY = AB = 5. Therefore DC = DX + XY + YC = sqrt(3) + 5 + 3 = 8 + sqrt(3). Special-right-triangle relations give the same projections without trigonometry. The two routes are valid alternatives, and the final segment addition fits the assessed scope.

figureEvidence.fact: AB is the upper base, DC is the lower base, and both sloping sides run inward toward the upper base; the perpendicular feet therefore occur in the order D, X, Y, C.
The marked lower interior angles are 60° at D and 45° at C, with BC labeled 3 sqrt(2).

audits.mathematicalReason: The first square has side sqrt(441) = 21 cm. Since the triangle is right-isosceles, its two legs are each 42 cm. Its hypotenuse is 42 sqrt(2) cm, and its altitude to the hypotenuse is h = 21 sqrt(2) cm. If the second square has side x, the triangle at B cut off by the square is similar to ABC, giving x/(42 sqrt(2)) = (h − x)/h. Hence x = 14 sqrt(2), and its area is 392 cm². Alternatively, the right-isosceles corner triangles give 42 = x/sqrt(2) + x sqrt(2), with the same result. Both proposed routes are valid; square properties and square area are used in either.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let h be the tabletop height, L the block's long dimension, and w its short dimension. The first gap is h + L − w = 32, and the second is h + w − L = 28. Defining d = L − w produces the valid two-variable model h + d = 32 and h − d = 28. Adding gives 2h = 60, so h = 30 inches; substitution gives the same result. The system-modeling scope and the two alternative solution procedures are defensible without claiming that a system is the only possible method.

audits.mathematicalReason: Every valid spelling ends at the central T in the bottom row. Reverse a path and restrict it to the left half, including the center column. Each of its six steps can go up or horizontally left, giving 2⁶ paths. The right half similarly gives 2⁶ paths. Their sole shared path is the straight vertical one, so the total is 2⁶ + 2⁶ − 1 = 127. This solution supports combined addition-and-multiplication counting and the overlap correction. Independently, assigning count 1 to each starting C and summing counts from preceding-letter neighbors gives center-column counts 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127. State recursion is therefore also a valid alternative, not an additional required method.

figureEvidence.fact: The diagram has seven centered rows, with C at both outer ends of each non-top row and the vertical center column spelling CONTEST.
Within either half, successive letters are reached by moving downward or horizontally toward the center. The final T adjacent to the S positions is the bottom-center T.

audits.mathematicalReason: Use brackets for triangle areas. Since G is the midpoint of BF, [ABG] = [AFG]. Because A, G, E are collinear, extending the common base AG to AE scales both areas by the same factor, so [ABE] = [AFE]. Also AF/AC = 1/3, hence [AFE] = [ACE]/3. Triangles ABE and ACE have the same altitude to BC, yielding BE:EC = [ABE]:[ACE] = 1:3. The parallel-line route is valid too: draw FH parallel to AE with H on BC. Then E is the midpoint of BH, while similarity gives CH/CE = CF/CA = 2/3. Thus BE = EH = CE/3. Both routes support the proposed proportional-segment scope.

The drawn intersection E lies inside side BC, so the requested ratio is an internal division ratio.
